Name: evidentiality_certainty_transfer
Title: Hearsay in the Weights: Does Grammaticalized Evidentiality Shape Multilingual LLMs' Certainty and Leak Across Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Some languages (Turkish, Quechua, Bulgarian, Korean) grammatically mark the *source* of information (direct witness vs. inference vs. hearsay) as an obligatory part of the verb, while others (English, Spanish, Mandarin) leave it optional/lexical. We hypothesize that (1) multilingual LLMs internalize evidential marking as a compact, causally-active 'information-source' direction in the residual stream that modulates downstream expressed certainty/hedging; (2) this coupling is language-specific in strength—evidence marked as hearsay in an obligatory-evidential language produces systematically lower asserted certainty and different reasoning/answer behavior than the same content in a non-evidential language; and (3) the evidential source signal leaks across languages, so a hearsay-marked premise given in Turkish contaminates the certainty/answer produced when the model is queried in English about the same fact, revealing that grammaticalized source-marking is entangled with the shared conceptual space rather than compartmentalized.
Related Work: Evidentiality is richly documented in linguistics and bilingual psycholinguistics: Aikhenvald (2004, 2014) characterizes obligatory grammatical evidential systems; Tosun & Filipovic (2025) show Turkish evidential marking affects bilinguals' certainty judgments and translation accuracy; Saratsli et al. (2020) study learnability of evidential distinctions. In NLP, uncertainty/hedging and calibration are studied almost exclusively in English or as scalar output-probability recalibration, and cross-lingual factual-consistency work treats disagreement as error. No prior work asks whether LLMs represent grammaticalized information-source, whether it is a steerable internal direction, whether it modulates expressed certainty in a language-dependent way, or whether source-marking leaks across languages. This differs from my earlier epistemic-certainty proposal (which concerns whether the model *knows* a fact, i.e., internal correctness) by targeting the orthogonal axis of *information source / evidential grounding* as a linguistic category, and from the cultural-default and grammatical-gender proposals by focusing on a source-of-information operator that directly governs epistemic hedging and reasoning behavior. It is the first mechanistic, causal, cross-lingual study of evidentiality in LLMs.
Abstract: About a quarter of the world's languages grammatically encode the *source* of information: Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua and Korean obligatorily mark whether the speaker witnessed an event directly, inferred it, or heard it from someone else, whereas English, Spanish and Mandarin express source only optionally through lexical hedges. In humans, this grammatical difference measurably shifts how confidently speakers assert and remember information. We ask whether multilingual large language models exhibit an analogous phenomenon and whether grammaticalized evidentiality is entangled with the model's shared conceptual space. Using minimally-contrasting premises whose only difference is evidential marking (direct witness vs. inference vs. hearsay), across languages spanning obligatory-evidential and non-evidential systems, we test three claims. First, we probe whether an 'information-source' direction is linearly encoded in the residual stream and whether a direction learned in one language transfers to others. Second, we measure whether evidential marking modulates the model's downstream expressed certainty, hedging, and answer behavior, and whether this coupling is stronger for obligatory-evidential languages. Third, and most surprisingly, we test cross-lingual leakage: whether a hearsay-marked premise presented in Turkish lowers the certainty and shifts the answer the model produces when subsequently queried in English about the same content, and whether the source direction fires during English processing. Finally, we causally steer and ablate the source direction to flip expressed certainty and to remove leakage. Across four open multilingual models we quantify the encoding, the language-dependent certainty coupling, its cross-lingual leakage, and its causal controllability.
Experiments: 1) Stimulus construction: Build ~600 factual/eventive statements, each realized in three evidential conditions (direct-witness, inference, reportative/hearsay). Render them in obligatory-evidential languages (Turkish -di/-mis, Bulgarian, Korean, and Quechua if tokenizer-supported) where the distinction is grammaticalized in the verb, and in non-evidential languages (English, Spanish, Mandarin, German) where it must be expressed lexically ('I saw...', 'apparently...', 'I heard that...'). Verify with native/MT checks and audit a sample; record a per-language 'evidential obligatoriness' feature. 2) Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B. 3) Source-direction probe: Extract mid-layer residual activations at the statement's final token; train a linear/logistic probe to classify the evidential condition (witness/inference/hearsay) within a source language and test zero-shot transfer to all other languages (report per-language accuracy vs. in-language ceiling and chance). Compute difference-of-means source directions (hearsay−witness) and measure cross-language cosine/CCA and whether a single low-rank subspace (PCA) captures source-marking across languages. 4) Certainty-coupling behavioral test: After presenting a premise in a given evidential condition/language, prompt the model to (a) rate its confidence in a follow-up assertion on a Likert scale, (b) produce a natural-language judgment scored for hedging (using a hedge lexicon/classifier), and (c) answer a downstream yes/no or QA item that depends on treating the premise as reliable. Test whether hearsay/inference marking lowers asserted certainty and shifts answers relative to witness marking, and whether this effect is larger for obligatory-evidential languages (regress certainty shift on evidential obligatoriness, controlling for resource level and translation quality). Include an English-embedded control that varies only the evidential phrasing to isolate the semantic effect from language identity. 5) Cross-lingual leakage test: Present a premise with a specific evidential marking in an obligatory-evidential language (e.g., Turkish hearsay), then query certainty/answer in English about the same content; measure whether English-side certainty/answer tracks the source-language evidential condition. Also probe whether the source direction is decodable during purely-English processing of the content. 6) Causal interventions: Using activation patching, localize where the evidential signal is computed and patch a hearsay representation into a witness run to test if expressed certainty drops. Then steer along the shared source direction to (a) flip witness→hearsay certainty as a manipulation check, and (b) ablate the direction to remove cross-lingual leakage, with specificity controls (no degradation on unrelated tasks) and fluency filters. 7) Ablations: layer choice, probe rank, steering strength, subspace dimensionality, robustness across the four models. Metrics: source-probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer gap, source-direction cross-language similarity, evidential-obligatoriness vs. certainty-shift partial correlation (Spearman) and effect sizes, downstream-answer shift rates, leakage correlation, patching/steering flip rates, ablation leakage reduction, specificity, and fluency pass rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Difference-of-means source directions may entangle the evidential *morpheme/marker* with the source *concept*; we mitigate with minimal pairs across varied lexical realizations, cross-content generalization tests, held-out constructions, and the English-embedded lexical-evidential control. 2) Certainty/hedging behavioral effects may be small or noisy; we use structured Likert and yes/no formats, hedge lexicons, large samples, and within-content contrasts (same content, different evidential condition) to cancel item-specific effects. 3) Evidential obligatoriness correlates with language resource level and script; we include resource covariates, stratify, and triangulate with the structural-control design. 4) A null result (LLMs ignore evidential marking, or it is cleanly compartmentalized with no leakage) is itself a clean, publishable finding about the separability of grammaticalized source-marking from the shared concept space and about multilingual epistemic robustness. 5) Some languages (e.g., Quechua) may be poorly tokenized; we validate coverage and drop unsupported languages, keeping at least two robust obligatory-evidential languages. 6) Activation-patching localization is model-specific; we report across four models and sweep layers. 7) Correct evidential renderings are nontrivial; we use native/MT verification and audit a sample.
